newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South Africa urges rethink of EU trade stance.
newsitem.headline: South Africa urges rethink of EU trade stance.

text.p: South Africa urged the European Union on Tuesday to rethink radically its approach to trade negotiations with Pretoria but denied that its own stance amounted to an outright rejection of EU terms for a deal.

Outlining for the first time the country's mandate, or negotiating position, officials said they wanted Brussels to address regional concerns and the need for "asymmetrical" trade liberalisation which would work in South Africa's favour.

South Africa's ambassador to the EU, Eltie Links, heading his country's delegation, said renewed talks on a trade deal scheduled for Friday and Saturday in Pretoria would be tough, but there was willingness on both sides to reach agreement.
"Our differences will inevitably raise eyebrows and raise tones of voices. What must be understood, however, is that there is an underlying seriousness on both sides," he told reporters.
This week's discussions should set the stage for more intensive and detailed negotiations later in the year, he said.

The EU earlier rejected post-apartheid South Africa's proposal for full accession to the Lome Convention which grants favourable access to EU markets to developing countries elsewhere in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.
In its mandate presented last March, the EU suggested instead that both sides phase out certain tariff barriers over a 10-year period to create a free-trade area.
Faizel Ismail, director of foreign trade relations in the department of trade and industry, said South Africa's mandate addressed several major concerns:
-- Any trade deal should be asymmetrical, with the EU opening up a far greater percentage of its markets to South Africa than South Africa would be required to open to the EU.

-- An agreement had to take into account South Africa's neighbours Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Swaziland in the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) who could lose valuable customs levies from a bilateral trade liberalisation pact.
-- The EU had to pay more attention to the impact of any agreement on the wider Southern African Development Community (SADC), which plans its own internal free trade area in eight years.
-- A package of development measures was needed to help the South African economy adjust to further trade liberalisation.

-- The EU should revise its current proposal to exclude almost 40 percent of South African farm exports from a future free-trade deal since such an exemption appeared inconsistent with World Trade Organisation rules.
Access for South African agricultural products has emerged as major bone of contention in negotiations, with European farmers fearing a flood of cheap fruit and other produce.
But Ismail said that while the farm issue was important, Pretoria's reservations went deeper.

Fundamentally, South Africa's preference was for a trade and development agreement rather than a free-trade agreement, since this would recognise developmental needs and the needs of the region, and accept imbalances betweeen South Africa and the EU.
Some 40 percent of South Africa's exports go to EU member states and more than one third of its imports are of EU origin.
